name: CONCENTRA GROUP HOLDINGS PARENT IN

devils_advocate.strongest_counter: That Concentra is a roll-up whose headline growth is bought, and that I have corrected the cash-flow base upward without checking whether the cash flow is real. This is the EFOR test from LESSONS: a serial acquirer's flat or growing revenue is purchased revenue, cash paid for acquisitions sits in investing activities where CFO-less-capex never charges for it, and a base built that way always reads as cheapness. Concentra acquired 72 occupational health centres in H1 2025 and over 240 onsite locations in June 2025, and 2025 revenue of $2,163 million against $1,900 million would then be mostly bought. If so, adding $77 million of after-tax interest to a purchased cash-flow stream compounds one error with another, and the +8% growth I am underwriting is not organic at all.
devils_advocate.what_would_prove_it: Cash paid for acquisitions against the change in revenue, and the company's own organic-versus-acquired revenue split.
devils_advocate.already_visible: Yes, and it clears Concentra — which is why the verdict is no_edge rather than rich. Net cash used in investing activities was $29.0 million in H1 2026 against $374.3 million in H1 2025, so acquisition spend has essentially stopped this year; zero centres were acquired in Q2. And the company gives the split directly: of the 11.8% H1 revenue increase, $28.7 million came from Pivot and $22.7 million from the onsite deal, i.e. about $51 million of the $124 million increase, leaving roughly 5.8 points organic. Volume is independently corroborated at +2.6% visits per day. The detector was the right one to run and the answer is that this is a 5-6% organic grower with real operating leverage, not a purchased top line.
devils_advocate.unresolved: The discount rate, which the schema cannot override and which decides the sign. Concentra's beta of 0.573 is measured at R-squared 0.145 on barely two years of post-spin price history, and per the LESSONS bucket study a weak regression attenuates beta toward zero and manufactures cheapness. At the engine's 7.12% WACC the market requires only +2.2% on my base; at a beta of 1.0 it requires +9.2%, which is where I actually sit. That is the difference between a large discount and roughly fair, and I could not settle it.

what_changed: Nothing that invalidates the model, which is itself worth recording. Q2 2026 (2026-08-06): revenue $606.0 million (+10.0%), adjusted EBITDA $140.9 million (+22.5%), patient visits per day 56,421 (+2.6%), with the increase attributed 'primarily to organic increases in both volume of patient visits and revenue per visit' plus the June 2025 onsite acquisition. Full-year 2026 guidance: adjusted EBITDA $485-495 million and FREE CASH FLOW $220-240 million. The acquisition machine has stopped for now — net cash used in investing was $29.0 million in H1 2026 against $374.3 million in H1 2025, with zero occupational health centres acquired in Q2 — so the free cash flow guided is available rather than pre-spent. Governance: a $34.65 million buyback of 1,000,000 shares (0.78%) from chairman Robert Ortenzio and related entities at a 1% discount, closed 2026-08-24, described as portfolio diversification; Matt DiCanio becomes CEO 2026-11-01 with Tanner Newton as CFO, the next step of a pre-announced succession.
consensus_case: At $34.77 Concentra is a $5.8 billion enterprise valued at roughly 12x the $485-495 million of adjusted EBITDA it guides for 2026, for the largest occupational health platform in the United States — 633 occupational health centres, 415 onsite clinics, ~54,000 patient visits a day across 46 states. The market's case is that this is a defensive, fragmented, GDP-plus end market with a genuine consolidator at the front of it: Q2 revenue rose 10.0% to $606.0 million, patient visits per day 2.6%, and adjusted EBITDA 22.5% to $140.9 million as the fixed-cost base levered. Workers' compensation volumes do not cycle the way discretionary healthcare does, the payor mix is employers rather than Medicare, and the 2024 spin from Select Medical left a levered balance sheet ($1.56 billion of debt) that now delevers into growing cash flow. The stock is up 22.3% in three months and 67.1% in a year, so the re-rating has already happened.
base_case_rationale: Eight percent five-year FCFF growth. The building blocks are visible and modest: patient visits per day grew 2.6% organically, revenue per visit is rising, and H1 revenue grew 11.8% of which roughly 5.8 points were organic once the $28.7 million from Pivot and $22.7 million from the onsite acquisition are stripped out. So call organic revenue growth 5-6%. On top of that Concentra is levering a fixed clinic cost base — Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin went to 23.3% from 20.9%, 240 basis points in a year — and is deleveraging $1.56 billion of debt, which converts EBITDA growth into faster growth in cash available to the firm. I will not extrapolate 22.5% EBITDA growth: 240bp of annual margin expansion cannot repeat five times, and the roll-up has paused. Mid-single-digit organic revenue growth plus decaying margin leverage plus selective tuck-ins gets to roughly 8%, and that is close to what the market is asking for once the enterprise value is discounted properly.
key_risks: READ THE SCENARIO GRID, NOT THE POINT ESTIMATE: the recorded fair value uses a 7.12% WACC built on a beta of 0.573 at R-squared 0.145 over barely two years of post-spin history. My own view sits in the +2pt (9.1%) column, where the base case is about -11%, not the +38% the point cell prints
Workers' compensation volume is a direct function of employment; visits per day grew only 2.6% in a strong labour market
240bp of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion in one year is the bulk of the earnings growth and cannot repeat indefinitely
State workers' compensation fee schedules are administered prices and can be cut
$1.56 billion of debt against $158 million of cash on a 2024 spin-off with a two-year operating history as an independent company
watch_for: Patient visits per day: a fall below ~2% organic growth would remove the volume leg of the thesis
Whether 2026 free cash flow lands in the guided $220-240 million range
Restart of the acquisition programme — and whether it is funded from free cash flow or new debt
Adjusted EBITDA margin: whether it holds above 23% or the 2026 expansion proves to be a one-off
